heuristics.rule: Use your own psychological and emotional state as a diagnostic instrument for relationship health
heuristics.condition: When you notice you have become chronically anxious, irritable, pessimistic, or unrecognizable to your former self inside a relationship...
heuristics.action: Treat that personal deterioration as a concrete signal that the relationship is damaging you, and seriously evaluate leaving
heuristics.because: The highest-upvoted answer directly frames personal psychological regression — hysteria, anxiety, loss of gentleness, pessimism, low confidence — as the primary indicator that a relationship should end, grounding the rule in observed self-change rather than partner behavior alone

heuristics.rule: Unresolved historical problems do not self-resolve with external circumstance improvements
heuristics.condition: When a couple has recurring, unaddressed issues and then external stressors (long distance, unemployment) are removed...
heuristics.action: Do not assume the relationship will stabilize; explicitly diagnose whether the core problems have been worked through, not just temporarily suppressed
heuristics.because: The poster's own 4-year case study shows that once long-distance ended and stable employment arrived, the relationship still collapsed because prior unresolved problems had accumulated and were never addressed

decision_factors.factor: Direction of personal psychological change inside the relationship
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Whether you are growing or deteriorating psychologically is a leading indicator of whether the relationship is net-positive or net-negative for you, independent of love or commitment levels
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare your baseline personality and emotional state before the relationship to your current state — look specifically for increased anxiety, irritability, pessimism, loss of self-confidence, and chronic exhaustion

decision_factors.factor: Clarity on why the relationship exists and what you are getting from it
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Loss of a legible answer to 'why am I in this relationship and what am I gaining' signals motivational collapse, which precedes disengagement
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask yourself directly: what is the purpose of this relationship for me right now, and can I answer that question clearly and honestly?

decision_factors.factor: Whether core recurring problems have been actively resolved vs. merely paused
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Unresolved problems accumulate and eventually become terminal; external improvements (ending long distance, career stability) do not substitute for internal relationship repair
decision_factors.how_to_assess: List the main recurring conflicts or issues from the past year — has each been explicitly addressed, changed, and stayed changed, or do they re-emerge?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: If the prospect of the future looking identical to the present is itself exhausting, that is a signal the current trajectory is unsustainable
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Visualize the next 2-3 years continuing on the current pattern — does that image produce relief or dread?

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying through repeated rough patches hoping external improvements will fix the relationship
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Years of investment (4 years, family introductions, milestone achievements) can be lost when the underlying unresolved issues finally surface as terminal, leaving the person with both the relationship loss and the cost of having delayed it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who are conflict-avoidant or who attribute relationship problems primarily to external stressors like distance or financial instability rather than interpersonal patterns

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting until you feel 'ready' or until conditions improve before addressing core problems
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Problems that are not actively resolved during the relationship compound — each unresolved cycle adds to the accumulated burden, making eventual resolution harder not easier
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Couples in long-distance or high-external-stress situations who defer difficult conversations until circumstances stabilize

failure_patterns.pattern: Repeatedly cycling through breakups and reunions without resolving the underlying issues that caused each break
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Reconciliation provides emotional relief and resets the pain of separation, creating a cycle where the relationship resumes before the root problems are diagnosed or changed — sunk cost and attachment drive re-entry
failure_patterns.consequence: Years of cumulative investment (4 years in this case, including family introductions) are lost when the unaddressed problems finally make the relationship untenable
warning_signs: The same arguments or issues recur after each reconciliation
Reuniting feels like relief from pain rather than resolution of the actual problem
External milestones (moving closer, new jobs) are used as reasons to try again without addressing the interpersonal pattern

failure_patterns.pattern: Attributing relationship distress to external circumstances rather than internal relationship dynamics
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: External factors (long distance, financial stress) are visible and changeable, making them easier to blame than diffuse interpersonal incompatibilities or communication failures
failure_patterns.consequence: When external stressors are removed and the relationship still fails, the person has lost additional time and emotional investment chasing a fix that was never the right one
warning_signs: Framing the relationship as 'it would work if only X external thing changed'
Making major life decisions (relocating, changing jobs) primarily to save the relationship without first resolving the interpersonal issues

diagnostic_questions.question: Who were you emotionally and psychologically before this relationship, and who are you now?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the relationship is producing personal growth or personal deterioration — a concrete, self-observable metric that bypasses rationalization
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you have become more anxious, irritable, or pessimistic: ask whether any specific change in the relationship or your behavior has caused this, or whether it is a stable pattern
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you have stayed the same or improved: examine whether exhaustion or confusion about the relationship's purpose is still present, as that is a separate warning signal

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you name clearly what you are getting from this relationship right now?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether motivational clarity exists — people who cannot answer this question are often already emotionally disengaged but have not consciously acknowledged it
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes and the answer is positive: assess whether those gains are consistent or episodic (good periods between bad ones)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: treat the inability to answer as a signal of motivational collapse and explore what would need to change for a clear positive answer to exist

diagnostic_questions.question: If the next two to three years look exactly like the past year, how does that feel?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Separates people who are in a temporary rough patch from people who have reached exhaustion with the relationship's stable pattern
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the prospect feels tolerable or hopeful: explore what specifically gives that hope and whether it is grounded in observed change
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the prospect feels exhausting or dreadful: treat that as a strong signal the current trajectory is unsustainable regardless of love

diagnostic_questions.question: For each major recurring problem in the relationship, has it been explicitly addressed, changed in behavior, and stayed changed over time?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether problem resolution is real or illusory — distinguishes couples doing active repair from couples in temporary suppression cycles
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes for most issues: the relationship may be in a genuine repair trajectory; look for consistency over at least several months
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no for recurring issues: the pattern predicts future repetition; assess whether both partners have the capacity and will to actually resolve those specific issues

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to know when to leave
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Waiting for a single dramatic event or a clear external trigger to justify leaving; looking for partner behavior as the primary signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Monitoring your own psychological state as the primary diagnostic — if you have become a worse, more anxious, more volatile version of yourself, that is sufficient signal regardless of whether a specific incident occurred
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Many damaging relationships deteriorate gradually with no single inflection point; using self-state as a metric catches the pattern before it becomes acute

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treating reconciliation as evidence the relationship can work; using improved external circumstances as rationale for re-entry
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treating each cycle as evidence that the underlying problems have not been resolved; requiring explicit behavioral change on the specific recurring issues before re-entry, not just improved conditions
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Repeated cycles without resolution compound the eventual cost — more time, deeper attachment, higher-stakes milestones reached before the inevitable collapse

community_misconceptions.misconception: Once the external stressors are gone (long distance ends, finances stabilize), the relationship problems will resolve themselves
community_misconceptions.why_believed: External stressors are visible and feel causal; removing them produces genuine short-term relief that feels like resolution
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: External stressors can suppress or amplify relationship problems but do not resolve them; unaddressed interpersonal issues remain and re-emerge once the external excuse is removed
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Couples who defer problem-solving until 'conditions improve' often find the relationship fails shortly after conditions do improve, having lost additional years waiting for a fix that was never sufficient

real_case_outcomes.situation: 4-year relationship with recurring unresolved problems, complicated by long-distance and employment instability; couple reconciled multiple times and reached high-commitment milestone (partner met family)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Continued the relationship through cycles of breakup and reconciliation, deferring resolution of core issues; ultimately ended the relationship after long-distance finally resolved and partner gained stable employment
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Relationship ended despite the removal of the two main external stressors; 4 years of investment and a family-introduction milestone were reached before the terminal split
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Removing external stressors does not resolve accumulated unaddressed interpersonal problems; if core issues are not explicitly worked through during each reconciliation, they compound and eventually become terminal regardless of how favorable external conditions become

psychological_barriers.trigger: Person frames relationship distress as being caused by external circumstances and expects relief once those circumstances change
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Motivated attribution — the mind assigns blame to changeable external factors to avoid confronting the more threatening possibility that the relationship itself is the source of harm
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Repeated deferral of the leave-or-stay decision ('once the distance ends,' 'once the job stabilizes') with genuine belief each time that the next change will resolve things
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask the person to separate the list of recurring problems from the list of external stressors — for each recurring problem, ask whether it has ever been resolved even temporarily during a good period, or whether it persists regardless of external conditions

psychological_barriers.trigger: Person describes feeling exhausted, anxious, or irritable in a relationship but frames it as a personal failing or external stress rather than a relationship signal
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Internalization of relationship distress — attributing the symptoms of a damaging relationship to one's own inadequacy rather than to the relationship dynamic
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Saying things like 'I've become so difficult lately' or 'I don't know why I'm so anxious' without connecting those changes to the relationship pattern
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask directly: 'Were you like this before this relationship? Are you like this in other areas of your life?' — anchoring the psychological change to the relationship context rather than the person's inherent character

psychological_barriers.trigger: Person has invested years, reached major milestones (family introductions, relocations), and is now considering leaving
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost fallacy — the accumulated investment makes leaving feel like waste rather than wisdom, increasing the threshold required to justify exit
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Framing the decision as 'but we've been together 4 years and he's already met my parents' as a reason to continue rather than a neutral fact about the past
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the sunk cost explicitly: 'The 4 years are already spent whether you stay or leave — the only question is whether the next year should also be spent this way'

reframing_moves.original_framing: When should I break up? (seeking an external event or partner behavior as the trigger)
reframing_moves.reframe: Look inward at who you have become — if the relationship has made you more anxious, more volatile, more pessimistic, and less like your former self, that change is the signal, not any external event
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the diagnostic locus from external (waiting for partner to do something definitive) to internal (observable, already-occurring self-change), making the signal available immediately rather than contingent on future events
reframing_moves.example_language: 你发现这段爱情里，自己不仅没有变好，反而变得歇斯底里，焦虑忧郁，一点也不温柔 — 'you find that in this relationship you have not become better, but instead have become hysterical, anxious and depressed, and not gentle at all'

reframing_moves.original_framing: We have so many problems but things will get better once [external condition] changes
reframing_moves.reframe: External conditions changed — distance ended, employment stabilized — and the relationship still failed; the problems were never about the external conditions
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Uses the poster's own lived outcome as proof that the 'wait for conditions to improve' frame was a deferral mechanism, not a diagnosis — makes the pattern legible in retrospect so others can recognize it prospectively
reframing_moves.example_language: 好不容易结束异地，他也有了一份稳定的工作，但是以前的问题堆积一直没解决，最终谈不下去了 — 'We finally ended the long distance, he had a stable job, but the old problems had piled up and were never resolved, and in the end it couldn't continue'
